Operator
On your telephone keypad. To withdraw your questions, hit star followed by two. This conference is being recorded. We're now ready to start the call. Sonya, please go ahead.
Sonya Ghobrial
Global Head of Investor Relations and Financial Communication, Diageo
Thanks very much. Good morning, everyone, and Welcome to Diageo's H1 Fiscal 2025 Results Q&A. I'm Sonya Ghobrial, Head of Investor Relations, and I'm joined this morning by Debra Crew, CEO, and Nik Jhangiani, CFO. Just to remind listeners on the call that in the discussions today, the company may make certain forward-looking statements, including those that refer to our estimates, plans, and expectations. Please refer to this morning's announcement and the company's UK and US filings for more details, including factors that could lead actual results to differ materially from those expressed in or implied by any such forward-looking statements. Hopefully you've all seen this morning's press release and presentation. For those listening to our webcast who'd like to ask a question, please use the dial-in details included in today's press release. With that, I'll hand the call back to the operator for your questions.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, that's star followed by one on your telephone keypad to ask a question today. Our first question comes from Simon Hales from Citi. Simon, please go ahead. Your line is open.
Simon Hales
Managing Director of Consumer Staples and Beverages Research, Citi
Thank you. Morning, Debra, Nik, and Sonya. Two questions from me, really. Firstly, if I could just ask you a little bit about the organic sales outlook into the second half. Clearly, you're still talking about sequential improvement. How broad-based, you know, are your expectations of that sequential improvement at the regional level? In particular, do you still expect to be able to deliver positive organic sales growth in the US in the second half, even as you begin to lap up against the successful launch of Crown Royal Blackberry? Perhaps associated with that, if you can talk a little bit about any innovation plans that you have specifically for the US market in the second half.
My second question was just around, you know, the H2 organic margin and EBIT growth outlook. You've clearly flagged, you know, sort of Nik, in your presentation remarks, the ongoing investment in digital route to market, higher stock costs, et cetera, are weighing on profitability in the second half. We are seeing hopefully that improvement in organic sales growth coming through, and we should be seeing more productivity savings dropping through in the second half of the year. I'm just trying to square the circle really as to, why that H2 profit growth forecast is a little bit lower than we might have expected.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Good morning, Simon. This is Debra. Yeah. So I'll take this and then, you know, Nik may wanna add in, particularly on the second question. First on organic kind of sales outlook. You know, look, we're very pleased to be back into growth. I would say when you look at that at a regional level, you know, in four out of the five regions, I think APAC is still an area, you know, and China specifically driving that, where, you know, I would say we continue to expect an outlook that is tougher, you know, just from a macroeconomic condition. That being said, you know, I would say everywhere else we're, you know, we would expect, you know, we're seeing momentum.
We're seeing that resilient growth in Europe and we're expecting that, you know, also to continue. I mean, Guinness is really doing very well, even though we are lapping now. This is the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. We are really seeing some, you know, good, strong growth behind Guinness, you know, as well as look in Eastern Europe, we're also seeing Johnnie Walker as well. You know, when you tick through, you know, Africa, despite the macro, you know, economy there, also seeing really good growth. You know, that's one where I would say once again, you know, momentum, they're navigating a lot, but we are still feeling about our ability, you know, really good about our ability to deliver there.
Things like the asset-light strategy really paying off for us when you look at how we're doing, in particular, you know, if you remember we just did Nigeria. Sales in Nigeria, you know, are really quite strong right away, off of the back of, you know, the improved distribution system that we're now part of there. When you go, you know, when you go in then to North America, I mean, North America, we expect to continue to, you know, to show improvement. Yes, we are lapping Crown Royal Blackberry, but of course, Crown Royal Blackberry didn't come in until about halfway through the half last year. It came in on under kind of limited edition where we are looking at making that a permanent SKU.
That will certainly help us as well as we do have strong innovation pipeline. We are feeling very good about the positive US momentum. That's putting things like the tariff announcement aside, which of course now has been paused for 30 days. I would say that that's helping us feel, you know, better about that outlook as well. This is why before the tariff announcement, we were saying we expected sequential improvement, you know, from the H1 into the second half. I, you know, would describe that as fairly broad-based. As far as H2 profit, yes, we expect those investments to continue.
As far as the benefit from those, things like supply agility, which is one of the main things that you would've seen our announcement on North America, that just came through on Alabama. That's an investment in the second half. That is not going to start seeing benefits really until fiscal 2026. This is why, once again, pre the tariffs we were guiding in fiscal 2026 and beyond to start to really see operating leverage with organic operating profit outgrowing organic net sales. I don't know, Nik, if you wanna comment on that.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
No, I think that's the critical point there, right? I think we truly look at the future from an angle of being able to drive, you know, true leverage through the P&L. That's what Debra said, you know, pre the tariff announcement, which obviously brings a little bit of uncertainty, but we're gonna find ways to navigate through that, and I'm sure we'll talk about that. You know, I think 2025, those investments. Remember, first, keep in mind there's the investments that Debra's talked about that will start paying out. We did also call out, clearly now, if you look at the H1, we are lapping this incentive piece that will also come through in the second half. Actually, when you pull that out, which is largely a one-off, H1 was slightly ahead.
I would say to you know, looking at the puts and takes, if you excluded that in H2 as well, that would probably be a similar piece. Like, you've gotta keep that in context, which clearly are one-off. I would say to you know, that's not the way we would look at it going forward, right? We would clearly look to offset that in here with efficiencies, with productivity and/or, you know, areas that we might actually pull back a little bit till we get back there. For us, it's really much more about phasing through what is some of the investments that have been made and those incentives. Clearly looking forward, looking for growth at a higher level than our top line growth. That's clear, and that will continue on through, you know, 2026 and beyond.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Oh, by the way, Simon, I just realized I left out Latin America. Latin America definitely has a, you know, clearly an easier lap from last year as we were destocking. I wouldn't forget about that. I also, you know, another benefit, speaking of destocking that we would have on the North America front is also there was some retailer destocking, if you remember from last year too. You know, there are some of those things in the background as well that just mechanically also help us. You know, we are feeling, you know, good about that, the, you know, the kind of broader-based momentum, ex-China, that we are seeing across the various regions.
Simon Hales
Managing Director of Consumer Staples and Beverages Research, Citi
That's very helpful. Thank you to you both.
Operator
The next question is from Sanjeet Aujla from UBS. Sanjeet, your line is open. Please go ahead.
Sanjeet Aujla
Managing Director of European Beverages Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Hi, Debra and Nik. Three questions from me, please. Firstly, coming back to the US, can you just talk a little bit about what you're seeing across shipment depletion from sell out? It feels like your sell out is running ahead of depletion. Are you still seeing retailer destocking in the first half of the year? Secondly, for you, Nik, can you just help us quantify the annualized impact on profitability pre-mitigation of the US tariffs, if it does come through and it's permanent? Thirdly, in your prepared remarks, Nik, you talk quite a bit about stepped up focus on operating leverage in the business. I think the Diageo's margin peaked around 32%. Is that a reasonable kind of benchmark to think the business can get back to in the fullness of time? Thank you.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah. I'll take the first one on the US. Look, we're not seeing destocking, you know, there was, I think, possibly in the appendix, I think we put in the one chart that showed the Nielsen/NABCA data, which, remember, does only track, you know, it isn't a perfect. 40% roughly of the US, and then our depletions and NSV, and we kind of brought that back by popular demand. What I would say is that now we're seeing between depletions, NSV and NSV, guys, these are running, you know, within a point of each other, so they're very close. Our depletions are generally running, you know, pretty close now, when you look on a brand-by-brand basis to Nielsen, you know, NABCA.
The difference there, you know, quite honestly, especially this time of year, is, you know, it depends upon how much the retailers bought in kind of prior to the holidays and then how the holidays actually do. Remember also, there's kind of the weird thing in Nielsen NABCA this year where New Year's Eve is not in December. New Year's Eve is actually in January data. That really makes a difference a bit in sell out. There's just some moving pieces in there. I would say, you know, talking to the team on the ground, they would say retailers were a little more cautious in their buy-in, but they wouldn't call it a destock or anything. It was more about just cautiousness going into the holidays. We really feel like that is, that's behind us.
Certainly, I'll just remind, like our inventories are at levels we're very comfortable, very appropriate for the environment that we're in. You know, Nik, if you wanna talk a little bit about the tariff.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Yeah. Listen, guys, it's a pretty fluid situation, as we all know, just given how the last 48, 72 hours have played out. If you look at the US, about 45% of our net sales of products sold are made in either Canada or Mexico, right? Just given the geographic origin requirements. When you also break that down further, the vast majority of that is tequila. Let me just give you some color on what we see today is kind of the gross exposure on an operating profit level. If you look forward now, planning from 1 March, so four months, we're talking about circa $200 million of gross exposure on operating profit, with 85% of that being largely on tequila, which is an industry-wide issue, right? Keep that in mind.
Now, when we look at the fact that this is not something that we were sitting back and waiting on, we were anticipating and scenario planning. We feel today we have good line of sight of being able to mitigate approximately 40% of that. Some of that would come in more immediately, and that's inventory management. I'll come back and talk about that in a moment. Some will take a little more time, and that 40% is pre any pricing decisions that we might make, right? I'll come back on that as well. On the inventory management piece, building on Debra's point, there is no stock build in our H1 numbers. In fact, particularly on tequila, when you look at it, the outflows and the sales have been so strong.
I would say back to Debra's point, I mean, yes, some of the distributors with the three-tier system, knowing that it's such strong growth, you know, would probably be looking at their levels, but nothing unusual when you look at our overall, NSV and depletions, right? All good there. What we did do was make a concerted effort as we went into the beginning of the year to bring in some inventory, and that's gonna help us as we look forward. The other pieces that we're looking at is clearly some supply chain optimization with the US team. More to come on that over time. The other piece also is we've already been looking at our overheads and what might we reallocate in terms of spend across various buckets and/or savings to be able to offset some of this.
The last piece, as I said, is the pricing dynamic. That's before, you know, that 40% mitigation does not include anything on pricing. The last time around, Debra, correct me if I'm right, I think when the tariffs were put in, we actually-
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
went with all of that on pricing.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
I was gonna say, last time when we navigated tariffs, I mean, we actually pushed it through 100%.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Right. Right.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
on pricing. You know, it's good to see that we've got mitigation this time.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Correct. Correct.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Before we even have to consider that. I think particularly in this more cautious environment.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Right.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Um-
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
That's not to say pricing isn't off the table, but it's just not the first thing that we would go for, given that we already have some mitigation. We'll look at the consumer environment, what competition's doing, but also I think gauge the timeline of which these tariffs might stay or not. Let's look at that too. I think we're gonna come back on that. Hopefully that's clear in terms of the impact. To your last question around, you know, what we wanna do and what we wanna drive in terms of operating profit, leverage, and the margin number. I'm not gonna comment on a specific margin target other than saying, I don't think there's any structural changes in the business that would preclude that.
Having said that, I think Debra and I are fully aligned around how do we grow our absolute dollar gross profit and dollar operating margin as opposed to just percentages, right? Because I think there are choices and decisions that are right for the business that we should be looking at that bring us incremental top line and incremental dollars that we're not playing in today. And that's ultimately what we take to the bank, and that's what we're committed to doing, as we look forward. Hopefully that's clear, Sanjeet.
Sanjeet Aujla
Managing Director of European Beverages Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Great. Thank you both.
Operator
The next question comes from Andrea Pistacchi from Bank of America. Your line is now open. Please go ahead.
Andrea Pistacchi
Managing Director, Bank of America
Thank you. Good morning, Debra, Nik, and Sonya. Two questions, please. Probably a bit more for Nik than Debra here. In the prepared remarks, you spoke about how you intend to improve the performance by applying more rigor in revenue management, in cost savings, in how you're assessing the returns on marketing spend, working capital to basically sharper, I think, execution in a lot of areas. How are you going to ensure that this really filters down through the organization? Do you need to change any processes, incentive schemes, appraisal process? And when do you expect to start to see some of these benefits?
Definitely for Nik here, if we dig a little bit deeper on what you'd like to do on working capital or cost savings, can you talk about where you see the main opportunities here for extracting efficiencies? The point here is that Diageo has had some strong CFOs over the years, going back to Deirdre and Cathy Mikells, and they've already done a lot on cost savings and working capital. Where's the incremental opportunity?
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah. Actually, Andrea, I'm gonna answer the first one on their operations. Look, I think there are so many opportunities. I think from the, you know, I've said this many times to several, you know, investors who've asked me. I think one of the reasons I was excited when I met Nik is I felt like he would be perfect for Diageo in this moment. You know, as he's gone out and looked at the business, you know, independently at times and then has come back, we've been super aligned on where we see opportunities. 'Cause to your point, look, we've had a lot of programs, but I will also say that there is so much more opportunity here.
I mean, revenue growth management is a good place to start. It's the top of the P&L. Beyond pricing, we've got so many opportunities in pack price. Our architecture, I mean, one of the things driving our great momentum in the US are things like small sizes. The 375 sizes that we've launched in Don Julio, in Reposado, in 1942, these have incredible momentum. That is helping us with that consumer that is cash-strapped right now, be able to afford our premium brands for the amount from their wallet that they wanna spend on alcohol. I think things like pack price architecture, quite honestly, in this industry, it's just kinda nascent compared to what it could be.
Promo optimization, we've got a lot of opportunities across the world there, as well as you know, even in trade terms in certain markets. When we look at COGS, you know, our COGS are still higher than pre-COVID levels. We do see, you know, our supply team has a big productivity agenda, and many of those things are starting, you know, we're starting to see, particularly around, remember, we've made investments in supply agility. Those benefits really start hitting the P&L in fiscal 2026 and beyond. That'll, you know, that'll be a big part of that productivity agenda. We also have made investments in digital. Things like the Scotch Intelligence Platform that's helping us optimize inventory.
You know, when you look at the amount of digital investments that we've made into marketing, and we already see everywhere we're putting these systems in, it's helping us. Everything from AI helping us do biddable media, helping us, you know, we have CreativeX that's helping us now reduce our non-working costs as we create thousands of, you know, creative around the world. To be able to test these, in some cases before you even put them on the digital platforms. A lot of opportunity in our creative development process, and reducing non-working. We, I think Nik mentions it in his script. You know, we actually have restructured. You ask about what do you need to do and incentives and, you know, structure, et cetera.
Our marketing team has actually moved into more of these agile brand communities, we're calling them, and conscious creative teams, helping us to more effectively produce creative that will be, you know, customized and appropriate for various markets. We can do it faster, we can do it cheaper, and we've already started that. You know, certainly, the team is very well incented around not only investing for growth, but also to increase the resilience and, you know, of both our financial P&L as well as our balance sheet. You know, I think, look, Nik's helped us in really taking a look and stepping back on, you know, you mentioned working capital, but also just in our choices and pacing of some of our other investments in CapEx.
The team is really behind that as well, which will also help us with just agility and, you know, and resilience during this uncertain time, making sure we make the right investments for the long term, but also paying careful attention to what we're seeing, you know, in the P&L. Nik?
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Absolutely. Well, I'm just gonna build on a few of Debra's points. The great thing is, you know, I think firstly, I would echo what Debra said. When I came in, I started going out, and every time I would say something to her, she's like, Yes. Yes, that's what we need to do. Margin percentage was a perfect example of it. You know, when I said to her, literally after four weeks of being here, I said, You know, great margin business, but it's almost in some way a margin percent obsessed business. And Debra immediately was like, Yes. And I said, I wanna focus on cash and cash margins, right? And actually dollars. And she's like, That's the way we gotta go. So there's a lot of alignment, as we've gone through this, right? So RGM is a great example, right?
Debra's talked about it, but I think what we're trying to do is now bring it together in a more, for lack of a better word, codified and structured way with sharing of these best practices that we can move on quickly, right, and build more central capabilities, marrying up with the local capabilities, right? I think that's one of the things that we've kicked off right away. I think when you look at it from an angle of commercial excellence, right? We both come from a consumer goods environment where I think we have a lot of opportunity to look at what we're doing in-store, but also on-premise, right? I was looking at some data points. You know, we've got now data for on-premise in 40% of our markets based on NSV.
Clearly, with just that data and the focus, in seven of those 10 markets, we've actually been able to drive much better metrics in terms of displays on menus, back bars, cocktails, et cetera. It comes back to when you have the data and you've got the focus, you go do it, right? There's gonna be a lot more that we're doing in that space. I'll actually look at our A&P spend. I think Debra's talked a lot about the A side and everything that we're doing on media, the conscious create teams, which are really bringing global and local teams together. That gets a lot more buy-in, right at the top. Efficiencies, AI, et cetera. I actually think we have a big opportunity as we also look at the promotional spend piece.
Are we getting truly the best returns on those dollars? Are we investing them in the areas that are gonna give us the best returns in a shorter period of time, right? I think there's opportunity there as we look forward. I think to your point around, yeah, clearly, listen, I'm not coming in and seeing that we've got a huge amount of space in overheads. When you look at overheads as a percentage of NSV, actually, Diageo's in a great place. That doesn't necessarily mean we're doing things as effectively, efficiently, and leveraging what we have.
For instance, you know, in terms of all our, you know, integrated shared service centers that are out there, in Bangalore, in Delhi, in Manila, in Budapest, in an integrated way to really leverage on where we want to have best-in-class capabilities that differentiate us and how we might think, for instance, around, you know, things that are normal to the business, but do we really need to have, you know, in-house. How do we automate that quickly before we start thinking about, you know, the ability to potentially think about what we do in-house versus outsource and actually use the capabilities that we have to have something to build out more differentiated capabilities over time. I do think on working capital, there are some opportunities. I think Debra touched a little bit on inventory.
I think as we look at our investments in maturing liquid as we look forward, we have to leverage what we have. We have the best aged liquid for sure, right? We've got to look at that from a positive in terms of what we can do on pricing to differentiate ourselves, right? We've got to bring broader pricing discipline into how we think about what we do each year, but also on the elements of how we think about the investments of laying down further and how we deplete and how we bottle, et cetera, and what we're holding in terms of, you know, what was, let's be honest, built on much higher growth forecasts. We have an opportunity to look at that. I think AR is an opportunity we need to look at. I think the procurement team's done a phenomenal job on AP, right?
I do think we have an opportunity on AR that I'm working with the commercial team on in terms of how do we actually build that in. You know, there's gonna be pockets of stuff in each of these areas that we're gonna go after hard, because ultimately it's about what are the things that we can do that are self-help with urgency and speed to help us build operating leverage, build more resilience to drop the P&L, and ultimately drive stronger cash flows to help us deleverage and get a more flexible balance sheet.
Andrea Pistacchi
Managing Director, Bank of America
Okay. Thanks for all this color.
Operator
The next question comes from Mitch Collett from Deutsche Bank. Mitch, your line is open. Please go ahead.
Mitch Collett
Managing Director, Deutsche Bank
Thanks. Morning, Debra. Morning, Nik. Morning, Sonya.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Morning.
Mitch Collett
Managing Director, Deutsche Bank
Hi. The US consumer appears, you know, pretty healthy in some other categories. I'd love to get your perspectives on why spirits overall remain soft. I appreciate you've done better than the market in recent months, but what do you think is holding spirits back? Is this still a post-COVID unwind, or is there something else happening? Which I guess leads on to my second question, which is I'd love to get your latest thoughts on some of the perceived structural headwinds for the category. You know, ready-to-drink, GLP-1, Gen Z, and cannabis, and I guess what seems to be a growing narrative around alcohol moderation due to health. Do you think those are real risks? And if so, what are your plans to offset those potential challenges? Thank you.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Perfect. Thanks, Mitch. Because you're absolutely right. Coming out of, you know, if you look at North America, and particularly the headline macro numbers, they are certainly improving, and I think give us, you know, a lot of, you know, I guess, cautious optimism, on, you know, wages are growing faster than, you know, than inflation and have been for some time now. You're seeing jobs, and, you know, I know in the latest jobs report, actually, restaurants and hospitality were the ones, you know, where the most jobs were gained. That's certainly good. You know, we are continuing to see and have continued to see for a while now, and just gradual improvements on sentiment. We've gotten beyond the election, you know, with a clear result.
All of these things were, you know, are quite positive at a headline level. I will say, what's holding us back, I do think, you know, you have to take down to the household level, and that's really where, and it's not just us. We're seeing this broadly across the consumer kind of industry in the sense that, remember, you know, we're still looking at. If you're a household, you're still looking at grocery basket prices that are at 30-year highs. Consumer prices, if you look across kind of all consumer goods, they're about 25% higher than what it was in 2019. Credit card debt levels are, you know, are increasing and have increased really since 2022. I think they're up something like 30%.
You've got borrowing costs because, you know, we're not seeing rates come down, interest rates come down. That means it's, you know, these are highest interest rates in 20 years. It's just taking a while for consumers to dig out of that. I think it's less about post-COVID at this point, but more about that, you know, call it the inflationary. As you know, as inflation has dug in for and has persisted all, you know, over a good amount of time here, people have acquired debt that now it's just gonna take a while to come out of. I will say, though, from an industry standpoint, we are seeing improvement. You're seeing across consumer goods, you're seeing volumes start to improve a little bit. Certainly, they're not as negative as what they were.
You know, when you look at the industry, I know I was saying six months ago when I reported on fiscal, our fiscal 2024, I said the industry was growing in low single digits. Volumes were down 2%. Actually, volumes now are starting to recover. They're down like a half a point versus being down to 2%. Volumes are starting to recover. Now, the total industry value has suffered because price mix has come down to kind of, you know, and help buttress up that volume recovery. This is where we cut differently. We are outperforming here. We're doing something different. Our volumes are also recovering. You can see in Nielsen, NABCA on a 12-month basis, you know, our volumes were down 2%. In the last three months, they've been down about one.
However, at the same time, our price mix is holding. Our price mix across this time period has helped, you know, us to grow, and that's because of the strong mix and premiumization of what we're selling. I think that's kind of, you know, when you take a look at what we're seeing in the industry, we still look at this and say, this is really largely more cyclical than it really is, structural. You know, the other thing I'll point out is the success of the small sizes, 'cause I think this really points to. I keep coming back to this because it just shows you, if you look at the category once again, and what's recovering in volumes right now in total industry is at the higher end, and it's because of these small sizes. It is the 375 and the 50ml of Don Julio 1942, which is quite an interesting phenomenon really.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Yeah.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Because you're still spending a fair amount of money for that bottle, but it just shows you that people, you know, are still a little, you know, cash strapped. That's what's helping kind of buttress up that part of the category.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
That's a very example of RGM at work, right?
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Absolutely.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Great.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Look, you wanted me to comment on the structural versus cyclical, some of those structural arguments that are out there. I mean, Gen Z, and we've talked about this before a little bit, there is a state of preference for moderation. That being said, we are still seeing household penetration for that generation +3%. They're coming into spirits, you know, faster than what millennials did. By the way, that household penetration number I'm talking about is household penetration for spirits. This comes back to the offset for us in particular, you know, even if their per caps are down, so to speak, they're coming into spirits faster. That ultimately is helping us. Look, every new generation, you know, there's different preferences and things that they do.
We see some of this kind of zebra striping behavior as opportunity for us, actually, particularly in several markets. You know, I would say Europe is really where we're seeing the most growth in non-alcohol spirits and beer. We're taking, you know, advantage of that, and that's actually part of our growth as well, is, you know, you have to think about the opportunities non-alc presents us. I think things like, you know, cannabis. Look, cannabis, particularly in some states now, has been legal almost 10 years. We've been able to look a lot at, I would call, the legalized cannabis market. You know, we really don't see a material impact outside of the fact, you know, that does take a percentage of their wallet.
It's just like any other, you know, consumer good. We're not really seeing a big impact, particularly on spirits. There is this hemp-derived THC that I would say, you know, that category that has, you know, exploded in some areas. What I would say about it is, you know, it's quite early. It's in this regulatory kind of gray area. Some of that's being bought in the mail and other things. You know, once again, it's gaining distribution, and the trial, anecdotally, retailers are telling us that, you know, it's probably impacting RTD sales more than anything else just because of the format more than anything else. There's a bit of a maybe a wellness angle to it. Like I said, it's early days on it. We're watching it, but that's what I would say about that one.
GLP-1, that's another one. Early days, we're monitoring it, but I think it's something like 40 million Americans, you know. Certainly you would expect to be seeing this in the data in a greater way if it were having huge impact. What I would say is it's hard to see a distinct impact from just overall moderation trends that we've been seeing and kinda following for decades, which is people wanna drink better, not more. There are some limited studies out there. They're showing not really a material impact, particularly for premium spirits. If they have an impact, it's more on, you know, volume kinda based, which is, you know, certainly not something that we promote, you know, within our industry.
Mitch Collett
Managing Director, Deutsche Bank
Understood. Thank you.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
I think I covered all. Yeah. Thank you.
Operator
The next question comes from Gen Cross at BNP Paribas. Gen, your line is open. Please go ahead.
Gen Cross
Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas
Good morning. Thank you for the questions. Hi, Debra, Nik, and Sonya. A couple from me. Just reading some of the presentation slides, it seems that you're pointing to more of a focus on cash generation, returns, and operating leverage, things like more rigorous review of CapEx plans and investments in maturing liquids. When I compare that to the messaging before, would it be fair to say this reflects a lower midterm sales growth opportunity in some of your categories? A link to this, I know you talked about some of the structural versus cyclical arguments a second ago to the last question. Could you just say if your confidence in the US spirits market returning to its historical 4% to 5 value growth algorithm has changed at all?
Finally, if I could just ask a quick one on the dividend. You know, consensus estimates are pointing to dividend cover being below your 1.8x to 2.2 target range for the foreseeable future. This is obviously, you know, before any potential impact from tariffs. I guess my question is, you know, to what extent does a dividend target cover really matter at Diageo? Thank you.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah. I'll take the first couple questions, and then, Nik, you can talk a bit about the dividend. I think, look, on maturing liquids, you know, remember that there's a couple things that has happened within that we've had to invest incremental money, if you remember. First is, coming out of the COVID super cycle, we had depleted a lot of, you know, call it the reserves kind of within that, you know. I think particularly on the Scotch side, there was a bit of a catch up. There was also, we had shut down some distilleries, at the early part of COVID as well. That also there was a bit of a recovery, of that Scotch maturing liquid.
That is, you know, call it a bit of a one-timer in the sense that it's making up for, you know, that super cycle. There was also, at that same moment, there's also been the acceleration of tequila, and particularly the acceleration of aged liquids. Guys, I mean, within tequila, things like Reposado is now 30% of the category. Of course, these things aren't aged as long, but certainly it goes into our, you know, maturing stock numbers. That build up, particularly as we were bringing in-house, a lot of the, you know, distilling and, you know, building up our capabilities down in Jalisco, that also had a massive impact on that maturing liquid growth. Then, of course, also even things like rum. We're aging rum as well.
It's not just Scotch, and then also bringing in, you know, and up the distillery in for bourbon in for Bulleit. There was quite a bit going on in the maturing inventory space. I think what Nik is talking about is he's really brought a nice kind of scenario planning around some of this because not all of this liquid is, you know, 10-year plus Scotch. Some of this is, of course, and in fact, a lot of these other categories, none of them are really that long. There is, you know, a bit more flexibility around that. Also, with the softness in volume over the last, you know, probably 18 months or so, it does present opportunities.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Right.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
That's the type of thing we're looking at. It doesn't necessarily point to lower growth. What it points to, though, is just optimizing that for the right time. What hopefully this assures you on is that we continue to look at that and make sure that we've got, you know, the optimal investment in that area. On to your question about, you know, NAM and kind of North America and kind of getting back to a mid-single digit, you know, growth for spirits. What I would say is, remember the things that underpin, you know, historically that mid-single digit growth. First, on volumes, it's really about, you know, total beverage alcohol and the LDA plus population that ages into that. That's a pretty steady trend for decades, and there's nothing that has changed in that.
We're actually not seeing, you know, Gen Z is a big generation, it's not a smaller generation. We're actually seeing, you know, from a population growth coming in, there's nothing that would undermine that. Spirits gaining share from beer and wine. You know, what I would say is most recently, it's probably been a bit more wine versus beer. It's also not, you know, sourcing quite as fast. Some of this is just the law of large numbers. You know, household penetration now for spirits is about 70% versus beer at 77%. There's still an opportunity, but it is, you know, I would say we're still gaining from beer and wine, albeit it's a little bit slower. Once again, that's only ever accounted for about a half a point to a point.
You have kind of on volumes, I would say there's nothing structurally there going on that would prevent you from getting there. You're already seeing, you know, like even look at our price mix for the half at 3%. I mean, that's a pretty good price mix for history. I would expect that for the rest of the industry, as the volumes start to recover, you will also see that price mix comes back. Anytime people are buying more whiskey and tequila, like they are in our portfolio, it does help overall price mix in the category. I will also point out things for us, like Ketel One Vodka is doing well, and that's certainly a, you know, a super premium vodka. You know, there's nothing there that I'm seeing that says it can't get back there.
I do think the caution is just in the broader, you know, consumer kind of macro environment. You know, it's a tough environment, and I think look, I think there's a lot of things that are gonna improve there, but it's just a matter of time. Then you wanna take dividend?
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Yeah. Well, in some ways, I think it builds a lot from what you said, right? I don't think, firstly, anything that we're doing to drive better cash generation means that we don't see growth, right? Just to be very clear, we would expect to see growth, and we would expect to see growth coming back. To Debra's point, it's more just about the short-term visibility issue, that you know we're focused, then, on what we can do. The big things that we should be doing are focused on cash generation, improving our leverage, making choices and decisions on where we allocate and spend money, being a lot more focused on returns.
I mean, those are all great things from a financial discipline perspective, which doesn't in any way mean that even as growth comes back, we wouldn't keep that focus, right? I actually wanna make sure that that's clearly understood. I think it's a highly, you know, cash generative business, but we can do more, and that's some of the things that we're focused in on. You know, we reviewed at length, and then made that active decision to keep that dividend flat. I think it's a prudent thing to do in this current environment. Having said that, you know, over time, we wanna remain committed to growing our dividend in a sustainable manner, and we'll also look to maximize total shareholder returns, which I think is a key priority for us, right? I think you asked about the dividend cover.
It's a fair point in terms of what it looks like. I think for us, it's much more around how do we grow that over time sustainably, but get the balance right as well with total focus on maximizing shareholder returns. I think that's all I would say for now on that piece.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Thank you.
Gen Cross
Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas
All clear. Thank you very much.
Operator

Managing Director, Jefferies

Your hands are slightly tied, you know, given this tariff overhang that's something, very, very dynamic. I guess if tariffs were to disappear, how do you think about a reasonable framework in the very broadest of terms and then perhaps relative to CPG? I mean, do you think you can grow at that sort of top quartile end of CPG, is the first question, with operating leverage? The second is on RGM.

If people are buying a little bit less volume, how do you ensure you get that volume throughput that's so important for operating leverage, you know, for the model to work? And then finally on the US, you know, clearly you're outperforming industry, but, you know, the growth is quite concentrated in, you know, two brands. You know, how do you think about diversifying your growth streams into the second half and beyond?
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah, perfect. I mean, I think, so, yeah, look, I mean, the tariff, certainly the announcement over the weekend did create, you know, a little bit of uncertainty about what that is. We certainly welcome the pause that then, you know, was announced in the last 24 hours, like, you know, on that. That being said, ex the tariff, and I think we said this quite clearly in the presentation, we would, you know, if that goes away altogether, you know, we were very prepared to talk about sequential improvement, you know, in the second half with strong market share. We were prepared to talk about fiscal 2026 and outperforming TBA, you know, with a modest sequential improvement versus fiscal 2025 with operating profit ahead of organic sales growth.
That is what we were, you know, very much prepared to do and so have talked about it in that, you know, in that sense. Also we have committed. I think this is important and maybe, you know, people haven't forgotten this or, you know, lost it in the presentation 'cause I know we put out a lot of information. You know, in the interim, until we can come back and give you more definitive medium-term guidance, you know, we are committed to coming back to you with more frequent updates to make sure that in this uncertain environment, we're giving you as much help and transparency as we can, you know, to help kind of bridge this gap of, you know, of uncertainty.
I think that's all I can really say about that. On the RGM point in small sizes, actually, we're not overly dependent upon volume. We feel very good about these small sizes. You know, these are great margins for us. They're great cash for us. I mean, you know, a 375 bottle of Don Julio 1942 is still $100, you know? It's a good business for us, and we feel good about it. I think, you know, on the US, you know, look, I'm very pleased with that, you know, aside from Crown Royal, I mean, first of all, Crown Royal, our largest brand being back into growth is tremendous, and we're gaining share of both the category and spirits.
Blackberry has certainly more runway to go as well as. You know, look, it is really stabilizing the rest of Crown Royal as well. It's been quite incremental. One, you know, it's one in every five kind of buyers is actually new to whiskey in this. So this is, you know, this is a great thing for Crown Royal. Also, you know, I would say that Don Julio and Casamigos, we're not done with those. I mean, Don Julio, you know, it only has a household penetration of 5%. So there's a lot of runway for growth there. Household penetration tequila is 33%. So lots of opportunity to build. Reposado has doubled. 1942, you know, has done incredibly well, but we still have opportunities, you know, in the rest of the portfolio, and you know, kind of more to come there.
Casamigos, you know, this is one that we brought, if you remember at the end of the year, we announced we're bringing it into our dedicated division. In stores, you know, this is a turnaround, so this is a process. But in stores where we've actually implemented the right pricing strategy, we are seeing improvements. We also have distributed the 375 and 175 sizes. Those SKUs are growing as well and helping us, you know, stem some of the losses on Casamigos. We are feeling good. We're launching a new campaign, I would say, on Casamigos. This is one also that gives us, if we can turn the tide on that would be an opportunity. I mentioned Ketel One is doing really well.
Certainly, Smirnoff in the second half, we've got some incremental innovation coming in. We are gaining share of Scotch, even though Scotch as a category, you know, is challenged right now. Most of that challenge is actually in the single malt area, versus Johnnie Walker is actually, you know, gaining share and doing well, particularly in Black and Red. This comes back to the brilliance of kind of Johnnie Walker is that we do span a very broad price tiers, you know, across various price tiers, and Black, in particular, is doing very well for us. We are also gaining share of gin category, and we're also gaining share in the cordials with Baileys. We are seeing from a share standpoint, very broad-based. What you are, of course, seeing is still an industry that's under some pressure.
You know, versus spirits, you know, that tequila growth has to come somewhere. But we do look at how we're doing versus categories, Ed, and we're feeling good that we are diversifying, and the team certainly, you know, has strong plans, you know, across our key trademarks.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
I'm just gonna build on a couple of comments that Debra made. I think you asked a question specifically around, you know, can we be in the top quartile of CPG growth? I would say categorically and absolutely yes. All right? There is clearly focus on getting back there. I think what I would read today's announcement back to withdrawing the medium-term guidance is more just around what Debra said. It's just the pace of recovery, and this was just exacerbated by, you know, the tariff announcements, which, you know, clearly is very fluid, as we've talked about, right? But, you know, do we see favorable long-term trends in the US and beyond? Do we see anything structural? No. It's just a question of timing.
To build on Debra's point then, what did we think was best now was to be focused more on the near term, particularly on things that we can manage and control, right? That goes back a little bit to stuff that we've talked about on driving better operating leverage and focus there. You know, what we're doing in terms of cash generation, et cetera, and more frequent communication, as Debra said as well, right? We'll be putting out a Q3 trading update on 19 May in advance of that mini investor event that we're doing in Dublin to showcase Guinness, which is actually where I'm gonna be trying my first Guinness with you guys. I'm excited about that.
Full year, we're gonna be out with you fith August, and then, you know, we're already planning for a Q1 trading update probably in early November. You know, there's gonna be several touchpoints where you might actually get sick of seeing Debra, me, and Sonya, but you're gonna have to deal with us, right? We're gonna be telling you more. I just think we have the ability to help, you know, shape the narrative as we go along, and hopefully continue to provide you good proof points of what we're doing to be able to take and manage what we can control.
Edward Mundy
Managing Director, Jefferies
Great. Thank you.
Operator
Next question comes from Celine Pannuti from J.P. Morgan. Celine, your line is open. Please go ahead.
Celine Pannuti
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Thank you, and good morning, everyone. My first question is on tequila. Barring the discussion on tariff, I mean, clearly you have what I would call an explosive growth on the Don Julio, and you mentioned the smaller pack as a help. How do you look at the sustainability of that growth? And why is it that maybe Casamigos has not done as well? And then a bit pertinent with tequila still, given the low price of agave and the high inventory of tequila, how do you see the pricing environment across different price tier evolving in the US?

Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah. I'll start with your tequila question. Yeah, we really have seen explosive growth on Don Julio. That being said, there is huge opportunity. If you know, you can look at that on Nielsen and see that. You know, look, I think we've got a lot of room to grow. I mentioned the household penetration's only at 5%. If you actually dig into Don Julio state by state, you know, which is what we start to look at, there's opportunities where we're still not number one in certain states and big tequila drinking states.
We still feel like we've got a lot of room to grow there, even though it has been, you know, quite a good run for Don Julio. You know, look, Casamigos, I will say, you know, a couple years ago, we were extolling the amazing things from Casamigos. It was growing at a 70% CAGR, I think, between fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2023, and one of the fastest growing spirits, not just in tequila, but one of the fastest growing spirits kind of brands ever. Absolutely also exploded. What I would say that, you know, within Casamigos, it was more of a Blanco. It was more of a 50/50 between aged variants and, you know, and Blanco. It's a newer brand. You know, we did not have the pricing strategy because of various out of stocks and other things that happened during COVID. Our, frankly, our pricing strategy as shelf for consumer got quite out of whack from where it needed to be, particularly on certain sizes. You know, certainly we have felt the impact of that. I think with the dedicated focus, I was in Italy and the team of what they're doing there, I think we're gonna see a much different trajectory as we look forward, in Europe and that premiumization play in spirits in particular.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah. France is a great whiskey market, and we are well underdeveloped of where we should be. Big opportunity there.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Mm-hmm.
Celine Pannuti
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Thank you.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Thank you.

Sonya Ghobrial

CapEx steady-state. What's likely CapEx steady-state?
Debra Crew

CapEx steady-state. Okay. Yeah. On your first question, you asked about sort of Scotch. Yeah, 45% of the portfolio, we talked about this tequila and Canadian whiskey. James Jones
Managing Director of Consumer Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yes, exactly.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Sorry.
James Jones
Managing Director of Consumer Research, RBC Capital Markets
Just it'd be helpful to know if 45%, tequila and Canadian whiskey, how much, just how much is Scotch?
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
I would say, just looking at the numbers broadly, to Debra's point, I mean, we're looking at Scotch and single malt as a percentage of US business being another 9%.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo

Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo

Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo

Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Ketel One. We've got Baileys.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Other things that come from Europe, and Baileys. There's other kind of things going on. We've scenario planned around all of them, though, and I think just reassuring, you know, everyone, we've kind of. We're also talking to people on all sides of this. Hopefully that answers that question. Then CapEx, steady-state.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
Yeah, just to give that point on Debra, you know, as she's talked about the broader piece, when we've talked about that 45% being tequila and Canadian whiskey, you're talking about roughly 60% to 65 in total when you think about non-US. So you're not talking about a big piece. In fact, remember, as I just said, Scotch and single malts is roughly half of that total, right? On steady-state CapEx, I'm ready to take this, Debra.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Yeah.
Nik Jhangiani
Interim CEO, Diageo
I think, you know, we're looking at this with the team, but as we get through this hump and, you know, leverage and sweat the assets more, I would like to see us more in that 5.5%-ish round number type of range of NSV going forward. Call it a 5% to 6 type of range, but we will continue to hone that and come back with a clearer outlook as we, you know, we look to reposition and reprioritize our spend.
James Jones
Managing Director of Consumer Research, RBC Capital Markets
That's great. Thank you both.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Perfect. Thanks.
Operator
We'll now hand the call back to Debra for some closing remarks.
Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Thanks everyone for joining today. You know, our performance reported today demonstrates that we're making meaningful progress even though the environment remains challenging and will likely continue to be volatile given the recent tariff announcements. As I said in the webcast this morning, we're firmly focused on what we can control. We remain confident in favorable long-term industry fundamentals and, more importantly, in our ability to outperform the market. We've shared today some of the actions we are taking to drive sustainable performance. This is an exciting time for Diageo, and we look forward to updating you in our more frequent communication as we move through the year. I also look forward to meeting with many of you over the coming weeks and at CAGNY at the end of the month. If you have any other questions, do let Sonya and the IR team know.
Sonya Ghobrial
Global Head of Investor Relations and Financial Communication, Diageo
Thank you.
Operator
This concludes today's call. Thank you very much for your attendance. You may now disconnect your lines.

Debra Crew
CEO, Diageo
Globally. It was a year of compounding impacts with inflation and a cautious consumer environment persisting following the extraordinary growth through COVID-19 and the related waves of value chain disruption. I believe these challenges are temporary and the consumer environment will recover over time. At Diageo, we are focused on what we can control. We've navigated volatility before and we will do it again.
We manage this business with a long-term view. We will continue to invest in our fantastic portfolio of brands and diversified footprint to maintain our position as an industry leader in total beverage alcohol, which continues to be an attractive sector with a long runway for growth.
